introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 5 : le sujet imprime « did the military intervene » (forme non standard), transcrit tel quel. Faits cités de mémoire historique (coup d'État du 25 janvier 1971 pendant la conférence du Commonwealth de Singapour, crise de 1966 et abolition des royaumes en 1967, Charte de l'homme ordinaire de 1969, mesures de nationalisation de 1970, expulsion des Asiatiques en août 1972, raid d'Entebbe en juillet 1976, assassinat de l'archevêque Luwum en 1977, guerre contre la Tanzanie en 1978-1979, chute d'Amin en avril 1979) ; le nombre de victimes du régime Amin n'est pas donné (les estimations varient beaucoup) et l'ampleur de l'expulsion des Asiatiques est exprimée par « tens of thousands ».

questions.enonce_markdown:
For what reasons and with what results did the military intervene in the politics of Uganda in 1971?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** On 25 January 1971 the army of Uganda, led by General Idi Amin, overthrew the government of President Milton Obote while Obote was abroad at a Commonwealth conference in Singapore. Amin declared himself head of state, and he ruled Uganda until 1979. The question asks for the reasons why the military took power and the results of its action for Uganda and Africa.

**1. Reasons for the military intervention.**
- *Obote's quarrel with Amin.* Amin had been commander of the army and had been close to Obote, but the two fell out. Amin was suspected of misusing army funds and was involved in the Congo gold and ivory scandal of 1965-66. Obote began to restrict Amin's powers, brought in a rival group of officers and reportedly planned to remove him, so Amin acted to forestall his arrest or dismissal. This personal fear was the immediate cause.
- *Ethnic divisions in the army.* Obote, a Langi from the north, had filled the army and security forces with northerners, mainly Langi and Acholi, and Amin's followers, drawn from West Nile and from Sudanese-origin groups, felt threatened by this rivalry. Ethnic conflict inside the army made a coup likely.
- *Obote's political record.* In 1966 Obote suspended the constitution, forced the Kabaka of Buganda, Mutesa II, into exile after the army attack on his palace (the army was commanded by Amin), and in 1967 introduced a new republican constitution which abolished the kingdoms. This made him unpopular with the Baganda, and many people, especially in the south, welcomed the end of his rule. An attempt on his life in December 1969, and the arrests that followed, showed the instability of the regime.
- *Economic and ideological policies.* The "Move to the Left" and the Common Man's Charter of 1969, followed by the nationalisation of a share of foreign firms in 1970, worried foreign investors and Western governments, and also local business. Some Western governments and Israel were suspicious of Obote and are believed to have been willing to see him replaced, although how much external help was given is debated.
- *A weak political system.* Obote had banned opposition and built a one-party style regime with the use of detention, so that the army was the only force able to challenge him. Corruption, a poor economy and the lack of free elections made a coup attractive.

**2. Results of the intervention.**
- *Political results.* Amin suspended the constitution and ruled by decree, with the army and special security agencies such as the State Research Bureau. At first the coup was welcomed in Buganda: Amin brought back the body of the Kabaka, who had died in exile, and released political prisoners. But the regime soon became a brutal dictatorship, with arrests, killings and disappearances, particularly of Acholi and Langi soldiers and of critics, including, in 1977, Archbishop Janani Luwum of the Anglican church. Many people were killed and many fled abroad, so Uganda produced a large number of refugees and exiles.
- *Economic results.* In August 1972 Amin ordered the expulsion of the Asian community, tens of thousands of people, many of whom held British passports, and he gave their businesses to his supporters in an "economic war". Because the new owners lacked skills and capital, trade, industry and tax revenue collapsed, goods became scarce and inflation grew. The economy was wrecked for many years.
- *Foreign relations.* Amin broke with Britain and Israel, turned to Libya, the Soviet Union and Arab states, and quarrelled with Tanzania, where Obote lived in exile. The hijacked plane crisis at Entebbe in 1976 ended with an Israeli commando raid, which humiliated the regime.
- *The fall of Amin.* In 1978 Ugandan troops invaded the Kagera region of Tanzania. Tanzania counter-attacked with Ugandan exiles organised in the Uganda National Liberation Front, and Amin was driven out in April 1979, fleeing first to Libya. This was followed by a period of political turmoil, and Obote returned to power in 1980, so the cycle of instability continued.
- *Effects on Africa.* The Uganda coup was one of many military coups in Africa in the 1960s and 1970s, and the long-lasting violence showed the dangers of military rule. It also exposed the weakness of the Organisation of African Unity, which, because of its principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of members, did not act effectively against the abuses.

**Conclusion.** The military intervened in Uganda in 1971 because of Amin's fear of dismissal, ethnic rivalry in the army, Obote's unpopular and authoritarian rule and the weakness of political institutions. The results were disastrous for most Ugandans: dictatorship, killings, economic collapse and isolation, and the end of the regime came only through foreign military action in 1979.
